# Introduction

Marine bivalves develop hemolymphatic cancer, or disseminated neoplasia, which can become epizootic. DN is manifested in an uncontrolled proliferation of neoplastic cells in the hemolymph —basophilic, rounded, aneuploid, with an enlarged pleomorphic nucleus. As the disease progresses, cancer cells infiltrate all organs and tissues, which leads to the loss of their integration [@Barber2004; @Carballal2015; @Odintsova2020]. DN is considered a lethal epizootic disease, although cases of remission have been reported [@Burioli2019].

As early as 2015, it was established that DN can be not only spontaneous ("conventional cancer") but also transmissible (BTN, bivalve transmissible neoplasia, [@Metzger2015]), and to date 10 BTN lineages are known, affecting 10 species of bivalves ([@Yonemitsu2025] and references therein). In BTN, living cancer cells are transmitted between host individuals through the water, like parasites. Each lineage has its own genotype, related to that of the "patient zero," i.e., the mollusk in which the lineage first arose as a spontaneous cancer [@Metzger2016a].

Despite a long history of research, DN has primarily been studied in exploited populations of key commercial species (see [@Carballal2015] for review), so its prevalence in unexploited populations and among the class Bivalvia as a whole remains poorly known. Even less is known about BTN, despite detailed regional studies in soft-shell clam Mya arenaria in North America [@Weinandt2026], common cockle Cerastoderma edule [@Bruzos2023; @Bruzos2026] and blue mussels *Mytilus* [@Hammel2022, @Hammel2024] in Europe.

*Mytilus* were among the first bivalves in which both DN and BTN were described [@Farley1969, @Metzger2016b]. Mussels are affected by two BTN lineages, MtrBTN1 and MtrBTN2, both derived from the Pacific mussel *M. trossulus*. MtrBTN2 is widely distributed and affects four mussel species including *M. chilensis* in the south of South America and all three found in Europe – boreal M. edulis and M. trossulus, and more thermophilic M. galloprovincialis. MtrBTN1 has so far been recorded in M. trossulus in the North Pacific and in Kola Bay in the European subarctic (in the later area, however, MtrBTN1-infected hybrid between M. edulis and M. trossulus have been recorded) [@Metzger2016b; @Yonemitsu2025; @Hammel2022; @Skazina2023b; @Skazina2023a]. The maximum prevalence of DN in mussels – up to 40% – has been reported in the northeastern Pacific [@Elston1988], and, according to indirect evidence, is explained by MtrBTN, although it is unclear which of the two lineages [@Vassilenko2013; @Skazina2023b].

The most detailed geographic data on disease prevalence have been obtained in Europe. The older DN studies of European blue mussels, which did not test the BTN hypothesis and were almost exclusively performed by tissue histology, were conducted in the Baltic [@Rasmussen1986; @Sunila1987; @Larsson2018], Black [@Ciocan2005), Adriatic [@Gombac2013), and Tyrrhenian [@Matozzo2018] seas, along the Atlantic coasts of Spain [@Figueras1991; @Villalba1997] and France [@Benabdelmouna2016; @Charles2020], and in Great Britain and the Shetland Isles [@Green1983], while the subarctic seas remain unstudied. All but the French studies reported non-zero prevalences below 1%, with a possible DN outbreak in Atlantic France aquaculture in the 2010s, when prevalences approached a few dozen percent ([@Benabdelmouna2016; @Charles2020]; but see [@Burioli2019]).

Detailed BTN studies have covered the coasts of Western and, to a lesser extent, Southern Europe from the Jutland Peninsula southward (the range of M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis), on the one hand, and the Kola Bay of the Barents Sea (effectively, the port of Murmansk; the range of M. edulis and M. trossulus) in the subarctic, on the other (Figure 1). For diagnostics, these studies employed genotyping for MtrBTN-specific alleles, usually in combination with cytological or histological methods of DN diagnosis. The average prevalence was found to be low everywhere, below 0.05%, with a maximum of about 1.5% on the southern coast of the Brittany Peninsula (Atlantic France), and is explained in the southwest and north of the continent by different genotypes and partly different MtrBTN lineages. In western and southern Europe cancers are represented solely by MtrBTN2 while in the Kola Bay almost exclusively by MtrBTN1 with only one case of MtrBTN2 recorded ([@Hammel2022, @Hammel2024; @Skazina2023b] and references therein). Further, all Kola cancers had mtDNA COI alleles identical to that in MtrBTNs from the Northwest Pacific while in the rest of Europe MtrBTN2 were marked by the other mtDNA alleles from the same MtrBTN2-specific haplogroup. This suggested that cancers had been introduced into the Kola Bay from the Northwest Pacific together with diseased mussels in the fouling on ship bottoms along the Northern Sea Route [@Skazina2023b].

In previous studies, reliable rapid diagnostic methods for DN and MtrBTN were developed for mussels from the Northwest Pacific and the Kola Bay — flow cytometry of hemolymph (FC) and mtDNA COI sequencing of hemolymph and muscle tissue (COI test for heteroplasmy), respectively [@Skazina2023a, @Skazina2023b]. Flow cytometry, in particular, quantifies cell diversity by ploidy, which enables the detection of a fraction of aneuploid neoplastic cells [@Vassilenko2014]. Sanger COI sequencing of cancerous mollusks reveals both the host genotype (mainly in muscle) and the cancer genotype (mainly in hemolymph) on the chromatograms, with MtrBTN1 and MtrBTN2 showing distinct sets of COI alleles. Heteroplasmic individuals carrying cancer alleles are classified as BTN-affected [@Skazina2023a]. It is important to note that both approaches may underestimate early cases of the disease [@Vassilenko2014; @Burioli2019; @Skazina2023a].

Here, we continue the survey of DN and BTN in M. edulis and M. trossulus in subarctic Europe begun by @Skazina2023b in the Kola Bay, now extending it to the White Sea and diagnosing DN primarily by flow cytometry and MtrBTN by COI genotyping. The White Sea lies in the very northeastern corner of Europe (Figure 1); its shores are sparsely populated, and the anthropogenic load is accordingly relatively low. The sea is quite rich in mussels. In some of its parts (e.g., Kandalaksha Bay), hundreds of kilometers of littoral zone are covered by a continuous carpet of mussels, and sublittoral beds reach biomasses of up to 40 kg/m². At the same time, these populations are not exploited, and mussel aquaculture is poorly developed [@Lukanin1985, @Berger2001 — to verify and add REF). We hold no prior expectation of either elevated or reduced DN prevalence in White Sea mussels relative to other European regional populations. Unlike spontaneous cancer, the incidence of BTN is not directly linked to the "carcinogenicity" of the environment, which is supposedly low in the White Sea, but is probably linked to host population density, which is relatively high. We only know that bivalves in the White Sea can develop cancer: in the only White Sea mollusk studied in this regard—the soft-shell clam Mya arenaria—a high prevalence of branchial pathological conditions resembling carcinoma has been recorded [@Villalba2022].

Our expectations for this study were as follows. (1) To find, in a large sample, at least spontaneous DN, since spontaneous cancer inevitably occurs. (2) If MtrBTN were to be found, we expected it to belong to the same lineages and genotypes as in the Kola Bay, located about 300 km west of the entrance to the White Sea and from where cancers may spread to the White Sea—that is, with a higher probability MtrBTN1 and, with a lower probability, the North Pacific "strains" (i.e., mtDNA genotypes) of MtrBTN2. Our expectations were not fully met. In the large sample, a single case of DN was found, which turned out to be MtrBTN2 with a mtDNA COI allele rather distinct from the North Pacific/Kola ones. We further characterized this interesting cancer by tissue histology and genotyping at additional mitochondrial and nuclear loci.
